Tool/function calling and structured output (JSON schema)
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-11-06
Start: 15:00 PST | Duration: ~48 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Tom Reynolds (CTO - Vertex Labs), Aisha Khan (ML Eng), Diego Marquez (Infra)
Shared: Deck: drive.redwood/vertex-poc (shared), Benchmark harness repo: github.com/redwood/bench-harness (SE to share), Security pack link: redwood.com/security/vertex

[00:00] Jordan: okay everyone thanks for jumping on, this is Jordan from Redwood, with Priya our solutions engineer. How's everyone doing?
[00:07] Tom: good, thanks. quick intro from our side — I'm Tom, CTO, Aisha focuses on model integration, Diego on infra.
[00:12] Jordan: awesome, goal for today is to scope the POC: define success criteria, get a sense of workload sizing, agree benchmark tests and timelines, and talk integration options — SDKs or OpenAI-compatible endpoints, function calling, structured output.
[00:25] Priya: i'll walk through a proposed benchmark and integration patterns after we hear workloads. quick note — we'll assume SOC 2 controls and SSO needs but we'll map exact docs after.

[01:05] Aisha: great. high level, Vertex Labs runs a conversational assistant that augments customer support agents. Typical session lengths are 6-10 turns, average generation length 120 tokens, sometimes up to 600 tokens for long context. Peak concurrent sessions about 120 qps at launch, expected to grow to 400 within three months. Latency target is sub-300ms for first token ideally, and full response under 800ms for typical replies. Cost target is also important — we want to be within X of our current supplier.

[01:52] Diego: infrastructure constraints — we need VPC peering, private networking; no routed traffic through public endpoints for the PII flows. Also KMS integration for key wrapping and audit logs.

[02:30] Jordan: thanks, that's helpful. So success criteria — I'm hearing: 1) latency targets (first token <300ms, full <800ms) 2) quality/accuracy measured by your rubric (Aisha to share) 3) cost per 1k tokens threshold 4) operational features — VPC, KMS, audit logs. Anything else?
[02:50] Tom: reliability/SLA and rollouts — we need canary and fallback to hosted if private capacity is constrained.

[03:20] Priya: good callout. For the POC we usually run two benchmark types: synthetic latency/cost runs with generated traffic and a quality/regression test using your prompt set. We'll provide an OpenAI-compatible endpoint so your engineers can switch minimal code. The bench harness supports both streaming and non-streaming APIs and also function/tool calling patterns.

[04:00] Aisha: on function calling — we heavily rely on structured JSON outputs for downstream tooling. We need to ensure the model reliably returns a strict schema, and we want a tool-calling pattern to invoke internal enrichment services. Can you support the OpenAI style function_call protocol?

[04:25] Priya: yes, we support OpenAI-compatible function calling with a few differences — occasionally the transcriber will say 'Open-AI compaible' — but the runtime supports the usual name/arguments pattern and also enforces structured output via the 'response_schema' option in our SDKs. We also have post-call validation hooks to flag schema drift.

[05:02] Tom: what SDKs do you provide? Our stack is Node + Python, some Go services.

[05:12] Jordan: official SDKs for Python and Node, and a Go client that's in beta. All SDKs expose an OpenAI-compatible surface (createChatCompletion / createCompletion semantics) and additional helpers for streaming, function calls, and structured response enforcement. We can share example snippets.

[05:40] Diego: network — for the private flow, we want to either use VPC peering or a customer-hosted connector. Latency over a peered connection is critical — can you give expected added latency numbers for a VPC Private deployment?

[06:05] Priya: rough numbers depend on region and hardware but for our Dedicated/Private deployments customers see comparable first-token latencies to hosted within ~20-50ms difference. We'll include a latency profile in the SOW and run a dedicated benchmark during the POC to measure end-to-end latency including network.

[06:40] Aisha: workload sizing — we estimate 120 qps at launch, 95% of requests are short (<=150 tokens). Peak bursts may hit 200 qps for short windows. How should we size the POC capacity?

[06:58] Priya: for the POC we'll provision headroom for ~2x expected peak: so target 400 qps for short responses to ensure we can exercise concurrency and batching behavior. We'll capture per-token cost, GPU utilization, and tail latencies. We'll also test with a larger 600-token/long-response profile to measure memory and KV cache behavior.

[07:35] Tom: sounds reasonable. Regarding caching — do you support prefix/KV cache to speed repeated context?

[07:44] Priya: yes, automatic prefix and KV caching are supported in the runtime. small caveat: cache effectiveness depends on session affinity and prompt reuse. We'll include a cache-hit analysis in the benchmark report. Sometimes the transcript reads K-Vick cache by our tool but it's KV cache.

[08:10] Jordan: cost modeling — we'll provide modeled per-token cost across different quantization profiles and batching configurations. For the POC we'll run two quantization configs: fp16 and a quantized int8-ish path to show cost/latency tradeoffs.

[08:35] Aisha: do you have prepackaged models or do we bring our own? We have a fine-tuned base model currently on Replicate.

[08:45] Priya: you can bring your model; we also have curated open models. For POC we can run your fine-tuned model as a model artifact in the dedicated pool or use a Redwood-hosted variant depending on licensing. We'll validate compatibility and performance.

[09:10] Diego: security — SAML/SSO, RBAC, audit logs, and KMS for key management are mandatory. We'll need to review SOC 2/ISO docs and penetration test reports.

[09:30] Jordan: absolutely — we'll attach the security pack and cert matrix in the follow-up. For the POC we can provision temporary test accounts scoped down with RBAC and limited retention.

[10:00] Tom: can we get request-level tracing and per-token cost breakdowns in the console?

[10:08] Priya: yes, Redwood Console exposes token-level cost and latency flames, and per-route dashboards. We'll instrument the bench harness to push spans so you can see traces in your APM as well.

[10:35] Aisha: back to structured output — we need the model to always return a single top-level JSON object matching our schema (fields: intent, entities[], resolution_steps[]). Can you do enforced schemas or is it purely best-effort?

[10:55] Priya: we offer both soft and hard enforcement. Soft enforcement uses response_schema hints and validator warnings; hard enforcement runs a post-process validator and will mark responses as schema-violating and optionally return an error or request a regeneration. For the POC we recommend soft enforcement with logging, then escalate to hard enforcement if drift is high.

[11:30] Tom: and for tool calling we want the model to call an "enrichment" tool that invokes an internal API; can you configure restricted outbound calls?

[11:40] Priya: yes, tool calls are managed — you define allowed tool specs and endpoints. Outbound connectors can be vended through the private network or webhook endpoints via the customer VPC. We can demonstrate with a sample enrichment tool during the bench.

[12:05] Diego: about the OpenAI-compatible endpoints — we will try to minimize code changes. How close is parity? Any gotchas?

[12:15] Jordan: parity is high for common patterns. Gotchas: streaming chunk shapes can differ slightly, and in a few cases parameter names for custom features (like response_schema) are Redwood-native. We'll provide compatibility shims in the SDK so your existing calls (e.g., openai.ChatCompletion.create) map to Redwood endpoints with minimal changes.

[12:50] Aisha: what about rate limiting and quotas during the POC — we don't want unexpected throttling.

[13:00] Priya: we'll set POC-specific quotas high enough for benchmark runs and provide scoped API keys. For production you'll use RBAC and quota profiles.

[13:30] Tom: timeline — what does a four-week pilot look like?

[13:38] Jordan: typical POC timeline:
- Week 0: SOW signed, access provided, sample data in
- Week 1: benchmark setup and smoke tests, initial latency runs
- Week 2: full-scale benchmark runs, quality/regression tests
- Week 3: analysis, tuning (quantization/batching), security review
- Week 4: final report and decision gate
So about 3-4 weeks end-to-end.

[14:15] Aisha: that works. We'll need a clear pass/fail criteria in the SOW. For us pass is: latency targets met in 95th percentile, model accuracy above baseline (we'll supply metrics), and cost per 1k tokens within agreed band.

[14:40] Priya: we'll draft objective metrics and include them in the SOW. Example: 95p first-token < 350ms, 95p full response < 900ms, accuracy >= baseline-2%.

[15:05] Tom: regarding logging retention and data residency — can we limit retention for POC logs and ensure logs reside in our region?

[15:20] Jordan: yes, retention policies can be configured per-project and region selection will be part of the POC config. For Private deployments logs can be kept in-customer region.

[15:45] Aisha: any dependencies from our side to run the bench?

[15:50] Priya: we need: 1) sample conversation flows and prompt variations; 2) representative request payloads; 3) a small set of ground-truth labels for quality tests; 4) network contact for Diego to validate peering. We'll send a template.

[16:20] Tom: let's talk about the benchmark metrics — you mentioned per-token cost, GPU utilization, and tail latency. Can you also give memory/kv cache pressure metrics and per-request trace IDs?

[16:32] Priya: yes, bench will capture GPU utilization, memory, KV cache hit rate, per-request trace IDs, token counts, and cost attribution. We'll provide a spreadsheet with the results.

[17:00] Jordan: quick note on fallback policies — we support multi-model routing. If the private pool is saturated we can route to a hosted model with maybe slightly higher cost but guaranteed availability. That can be a part of your rollout strategy.

[17:25] Diego: good. For audit purposes we need to see who triggered model updates and access to rollout history.

[17:32] Priya: Console includes rollout history, who changed what, and you can tie it to SSO identities. We'll include a screenshot in the SOW.

[18:00] Aisha: any concerns about hallucinations and guardrails?

[18:10] Priya: we'll run safety/regression tests during bench and show how to use tool calling to ground the model. Also the response_schema enforcement reduces hallucination surface for structured outputs.

[18:35] Tom: ok let's summarize next steps and owners.

[18:40] Jordan: recap: Redwood sends SOW + pricing + security docs by Monday 2025-11-10. Priya sends benchmark harness and example payloads by Friday 2025-11-07. Vertex provides sample dataset and network contact by 2025-11-12. Schedule benchmark week of 2025-11-17.

[19:00] Diego: noted. We'll also confirm whether to use our fine-tuned model artifact or host it with Redwood. Diego will check licensing and infra constraints.

[19:20] Aisha: one last detail — for function calling we need limited outbound to internal enrichment; will need a short security approval path. We'll start that in parallel.

[19:35] Jordan: great. Anything else?

[19:40] Tom: no, that covers it. Thanks Jordan and Priya.

[19:45] Jordan: thanks everyone, we'll follow up with the SOW and links.

[47:30] call end (approx)

Notes on transcript quality: occasional mis-transcriptions (e.g., K-Vick cache -> KV cache, Open-AI compaible -> OpenAI-compatible), and some speaker label noise. The transcript preserves conversational flow with natural interruptions and clarifications.
